editorialDecl.p: The text is transcribed as printed. Spelling, capitalisation and punctuation follow the source, including period forms such as Honorable, plebian, Clarionets and Maygars, and the Scots dialect of the ballads. Words wholly in capitals or small capitals in the source are transcribed in the case printed. Small capitals, italics, blackletter, script and letter-spaced faces are recorded with rendition pointers to the definitions in tagsDecl.

Ditto marks (,,) in the orchestra list are kept and expanded with choice. The dagger sigil (†) marking Conservatorium players is kept as printed. Long rules, dotted separators and printer's ornaments are recorded as milestone or figure elements. Printed page numbers are recorded as fw. Line breaks within prose are not recorded; verse lines are.
Page breaks carry the sequence number of the page in the digitised copy (1 to 20) in n and point to the matching surface in the facsimile.

lg.l: “O WHERE hae ye been, my long lost lover,
This seven lang years and mair?”
“ O I'm come again to seek your love,
An' the vows that ye did swear.”
“ Now haud your tongue o' my love and vows,
For they can breed but strife;
Now haud your tongue o' my former vows,
For I am anither man's wife.”
“ O fause are the vows o' womankind,
But fair is their fause bodie;
I wad never hae trodden on Irish ground,
Were it no for the love o' thee.”
“ Ye may leave your husband to himsel',
And sail wi' me across the sea,
Sae fair the wind doth blow.”
“ See ye not seven pretty ships,
The eighth brought me to land,
“ There's mantles warm to wrap my love,
O' the silk and soft velvet,
And rich attires to deck her head,
And costly shoon for her feet.”
“ O how do you like the ship?” he said,
“ Or how do you like the sea?
And how do you like the bold mariners
That wait upon thee and me?”
“ O weel I like the ship,” she said,
“ And weel I like the sea,
But where are a' your mariners?
I see nane but thee and me.”
They hadna sailed a league, a league,
When eerie grew the lift above,
She hadna sailed a league, a league,
When she espied the cloven hoof,
“ O what are yon, yon pleasant hills,
That the sun shines sweetly on?”
“ O yon are the hills of heaven,” he said
“ O whatna mountain is yon,” she said,
“ Sae dreary wi' frost and snow?”
“ O yon is the mountain o' hell,” he cried,
“ Where you and I maun go.”
The clouds grew black, and the wind grew loud,
And the levin filled her e'e;
And waesome wailed the snow-white sprites,
He struck the mainmast wi' his hand,
He split the gallant ship in twain,
And sank her in the sea.

div.note: This occurs in Act III, Scene 2, where the disconcerted pair of lovers, weary with their vain flight, sink to the ground, and by the chorus of Puck, are lulled into an enchanted sleep.

note.p: Life presented itself to the Greek mind as a series of manifestations of Power Omnipotent, irresistible, irrevocable, first in the order of forces, loomed Fate, then the gods, the ancestral heroes, and the pre-eminent men of the times. Each State, surrounded by enemies, depended for its safety on the courage and power of its citizens, whom a reverse of war would convert into slaves with their wives and children. The actual experience of the Power and Tragedy of human existence, which to our modern comfortable plebian semi-vegetable life are almost unintelligible, lent an intensity to the moment which we can but faintly imagine. Power and its limitation were equally displayed in the sudden plunge from the height of prosperity to the depth of woe, and found expression in the never equalled strength and restraint of Greek art, imparting a reverential solemnity even to its most joyous utterances. This is the key note of their art, energetic power, and fate:

lg.l: Fate, whose horizons, narrowing from afar
Within their blind abysmal night immerse
Both gods and men, and all things else that be

note.p: In the following ode from Goethe's masterpiece, these qualities are passionately felt by one who was himself a Greek at heart though born in a barbarian age. The music is an endeavour to complete and enforce the poet's intention. The serenity, not untinged with a certain noble sadness, of the first stanza, is contrasted with those following, in which the power and majesty and terrible presence of the gods is imaged, to which succeeds the picture of limited fettered humanity.

note.p: In the Passacaglia we see, from a single idea by a development gradual, but resistless as fate, the growth of a huge superstructure almost overpowering in its nobility and grandeur, suggesting the unfolding of some mighty work of nature herself
When the watery ear-tickling organ music of the present age will have vanished into oblivion, such works as this will stand as the eternal monument to the imperishable glory of Bach.

In the wonderfully expressive and characteristic music of the Hungarians we find preserved the nobler and more significant phases of the Dance, before it had been corrupted by civilised larrikinism, and whilst it still remained among the people at large the one means through which their natural feelings and instincts found expression. (12)
Not only at one time was the Dance a religious rite, but also it fulfilled the present office of the drama, and became an artistic representation of human passion and action. In the course of the various figures through which the dancers went, the joy and woe, love and hate, hope and despair, of mankind were represented. Youths would woo and maidens would play the coquette.

In Brahms' music we find not only those poetical moods which it once was the object of the dance to portray, but a delightful suggestion of the picturesque character of the people, and the free, wild naïve aspect of Nature, which nowhere assumes a more beautiful or striking aspect than in the country of the Maygars.

lg.l: IF a youth should meet a maiden,
Need she run away with fright;
If his looks should win her favour,
Sure the girl may use her sight.
Tho' she must, in maiden manner,
Where's the harm, if she, unnoticed,
Strive a sidelong look to steal.
I no guilt therein can find;
Tho' her cheeks may blush a little,
Yet it will not strike her blind.
Looks are followed soon by sighs;
He sighs fairest, she smiles dearest,
Soon a marriage we will see.
Would you like to see me bride?
Am I not a pretty maiden,
And he is a smart young boy.

lg.l: A CHIEFTAIN to the highlands bound
And I'll give thee a silver pound
To row us o'er the ferry.”
“ Now who be ye would cross Lochgyle
“ Oh, I'm the chief of Ulvas' Isle,
And fast before her father's men,
And should he find us in the glen,
My blood would stain the heather.
His horsemen hard behind us ride;
Then who will cheer my bonny bride,
When they have slain her lover?
Out spake the hardy highland wight,
“ I'll go, my chief, I'm ready!
It is not for your silver bright,
And by my word, the bonny bird
So though the waves are raging white,
I'll row you o'er the ferry.”
By this the storm grew loud apace,
And in the scowl of heaven each face
Grew dark as they were speaking.
But still as wilder blew the wind,
And as the night grew drearer,
Adown the glen rode armed men,
“ Oh haste thee, haste!” the lady cries,
I'll meet the raging of the skies,
The boat has left the stormy land,
When, oh, too strong for human hand,
And still they rowed amidst the roar
Lord Ullin reached the fatal shore,
His wrath was changed to wailing.
For sore dismayed, thro' storm and shade,
One lovely arm she stretched for aid,
And one was round her lover.
“ Come back, come back!” he cried in grief
And I'll forgive your Highland chief,
'Twas vain: the loud waves lashed the shore,
The waters wild went o'er his child,
